food.text: The Tollund Man was hanged in Denmark between 405 and 384 BC, with a plaited hide noose drawn tight around his neck. His body was left in a Jutland bog that preserved it so well that his last meal could be studied. His stomach and intestines held remains from approximately 40 identifiable plant species, and barley formed the principal ingredient.

The Iron Age in Scandinavia brought rapid and deep change to the way of life. Agricultural production became more intensified, organized around larger settlements and much more labour-intensive. Slaves were introduced and deployed, something uncommon in the Nordic Bronze Age.

Traces of prehistoric field systems found in places such as Denmark, Sweden, Poland and the Baltic states are known as Celtic fields. They can date from the Early Bronze Age, c. 1800 BC, until the early medieval period.

Physicians who examined Tollund Man concluded from the stage of digestion that he had eaten approximately 12 to 24 hours before he was hanged. Alongside the barley, researchers found small quantities of corn spurrey, false flax, knotgrass and several plants associated with wetland environments. A 2021 analysis also found eggs of whipworm, tapeworm and roundworm in his intestines, so he carried intestinal parasites when he died.

Before the Iron Age changes, herds of livestock had grazed freely in large wood pastures. They were now placed in stables, probably to use manure more efficiently and increase agricultural production.
Celtic fields were divided into a patchwork of square plots rarely more than 2,000 m2 in area. Their small size, 35 to 50 m across, implies that each was cultivated by a single person or household.

Tollund Man's last meal also contained weed seeds, grains of sand and other threshing waste that would normally have been removed when harvested barley was given its final cleaning. Researchers could not tell whether this reflected deliberate ritual practice, ordinary food preparation or accidental contamination.

At the upper and lower ends of Celtic fields, archaeologists can often see lynchets, which are evidence of early ploughing. The fields are sometimes preserved as earthworks or soil marks in areas where industrial farming has not been adopted.

Agricultural villages such as Vorbasse in Denmark are known from the period 200 to 400 AD. Northern Europe entered the protohistorical period in the early centuries AD, when Roman authors began to write ethnographic accounts of it.

The name Celtic field was given by O. G. S. Crawford, yet the fields themselves are not related to the Celtic culture. They are found in proximity to other ancient features such as enclosures, sunken lanes and farmsteads.

art.text: The Gundestrup cauldron is a richly decorated silver vessel thought to date to the 1st century BC. It is the largest known example of European silver work from its period, and the silversmithing of its plates is very skilled. It is now in the National Museum of Denmark.

From the 4th century CE, a continuous artistic tradition common to most of north-western Europe took shape. Scandinavian artists focused broadly on varieties of convoluted animal ornamentation, used to decorate a wide variety of objects. This tradition became the foundation on which Viking Age art was later built.

Several Bronze Age motifs, such as the wheel cross, reappear in later Iron Age contexts in Scandinavia. This happened even though the putatively solar-oriented belief system of Bronze Age Scandinavia is believed to have died out around 500 BCE.
The Gundestrup cauldron was found in 1891 in a peat bog near the hamlet of Gundestrup in north-eastern Jutland.

The style and workmanship of the Gundestrup cauldron suggest a Thracian origin, while its imagery seems Celtic. Because of this mix, the silver vessel found in Denmark may not reflect local styles at all, and it is described as a possibly alien find.

war.text: Between 113 and 101 BC, two Germanic tribes from Jutland, the Cimbri and the Teutons, attacked the Roman Republic in what is now known as the Cimbrian War. They initially inflicted the heaviest losses that Rome had suffered since the Second Punic War. Roman legions eventually defeated both tribes.

In 113–101 BC two Germanic tribes from Jutland, in modern-day Denmark, attacked the Roman Republic in what is known as the Cimbrian War. The Cimbri and the Teutons initially inflicted the heaviest losses Rome had suffered since the Second Punic War. They were eventually defeated by the Roman legions.

In the early centuries of the Common Era, huge numbers of destroyed weapons were placed in wetlands in Scandinavia. They were mostly spears and swords, but also shields, tools and other equipment. The precise purposes of these depositions are unclear.

Through the 5th and 6th centuries, gold and silver became more common in Scandinavia. Much of this can be attributed to Germanic tribes ransacking the Roman Empire, from which many Scandinavians returned with gold and silver.

Bog bodies found in Denmark, Schleswig and southern Sweden were buried together with weapons, household wares and woollen clothes. Great ships made for rowing have been found from the 4th century in Nydam mosse in Schleswig.

In the early centuries of the Common Era, huge numbers of destroyed weapons were placed in Scandinavian wetlands. Beginning in the 5th century, the deposits changed, and fibulae and bracteates were placed in or beside wetlands instead. The precise purposes of such depositions are unclear.

Beginning in the 5th century, the nature of Scandinavian wetland deposits changed. Fibulae and bracteates were placed in or beside wetlands from the 5th to the mid-6th centuries, after the earlier centuries of deposited weapons.
Bronze could not be produced in Scandinavia because tin was not a local resource. Iron production from bog iron, mostly in Denmark, slowly gained ground, and iron was suitable for tools and weapons.

In the 6th and 5th centuries BC, ever-increasing conflicts and wars between the central European Celtic tribes and the Mediterranean cultures destabilized the old trade routes between Scandinavia and the Mediterranean, eventually breaking them down. Archaeology attests a rapid and deep change in Scandinavian culture and way of life. Slaves were introduced and deployed, something uncommon in the Nordic Bronze Age, and agricultural production became more intensive and far more labour-intensive. The article calls the advent of the Iron Age in Scandinavia a time of great crisis.

literature.text: The most northerly place named in ancient Greek and Roman literature was Thule. The Greek explorer Pytheas of Massalia first wrote of it in about 320 BC. Later writers often called it an island north of Ireland or Britain, though Pytheas never explicitly described it as one.

In classical and medieval literature, the Latin phrase ultima Thule, meaning "farthest Thule", took on a metaphorical meaning. It came to stand for any distant place beyond the "borders of the known world". A real northern place became a lasting literary image.

The earliest identified source for the name Scandinavia is Pliny the Elder's Natural History, dated to the 1st century AD. The name is thought to go back to a Proto-Germanic compound, which appears in Old Norse as Skáney and is also linked to the name of Scania.

The Roman poet Silius Italicus (AD 25 to 101) wrote that the people of Thule were painted blue. He pictured them driving scythe-bearing chariots into battle. This suggests a link to the Picts, whose name comes from the Latin pictus, meaning "painted".

Modern scholars have proposed many real places for Thule, including Orkney, Shetland, the Faroe Islands and Iceland. Two candidates lie in Scandinavia and the Baltic: the island of Saaremaa in Estonia and the Norwegian island of Smøla. Ancient writers left too little detail to settle the question.

The third-century Latin grammarian Gaius Julius Solinus described Thule in his Polyhistor. He said it lay a voyage of five days and nights from Orkney. He also wrote that it was fruitful, with a lasting yield of crops.

Tacitus wrote in the 1st century AD about Nerthus, a Germanic fertility god, in his Germania. Scholars have pointed out similarities between Nerthus and Njörðr, a Vanir god of Old Norse literature. This links a Roman text to later Scandinavian myth.

science.text: Iron metallurgy began to be practised in Scandinavia during the later Bronze Age, from at least the 9th century BC. Around the 5th century BC, the Nordic Bronze Age was succeeded by the Pre-Roman Iron Age.
Great ships made for rowing have been found from the 4th century in Nydam mosse in Schleswig. They show the shipbuilding skill of the Scandinavian peoples in the later Classical period.
The Iron Age in Scandinavia began around 500 BC with the Jastorf culture. Ferrous metallurgy arrived through contact with the Hallstatt D and La Tène cultures.

In the 6th and 5th centuries BC, ever-increasing conflicts and wars between the central European Celtic tribes and the Mediterranean cultures destabilized the old major trade routes linking Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, and eventually broke them down. The arrival of the Iron Age in Scandinavia was a time of great crisis. Even so, the population grew and new technology was developed. The period may reflect a change of culture rather than a decline in standards of living.

During the early Iron Age, Scandinavian livestock that had once grazed freely in large wood pastures were placed in stables. This was probably done to use manure more efficiently and increase agricultural production.

Agricultural production in Iron Age Scandinavia became more intensive, organized around larger settlements and far more labour-intensive. Slaves, uncommon in the Nordic Bronze Age, were introduced and put to work.

politics.text: The royal dynasty of the Swedes, the Yngling, was founded in the 5th century. Based at Gamla Uppsala, the Ynglings would come to dominate much of Scandinavia.

Norway was inhabited by a large number of North Germanic tribes and divided into a score of petty kingdoms. Archaeological evidence suggests that a warrior elite continued to dominate North Germanic society into the Early Middle Ages.

Roman geographers described a region called Germania that stretched roughly from the Rhine in the west to the Vistula in the east. Its northern edge reached the known parts of southern Scandinavia, so the Romans saw the far north as part of the Germanic world.

According to the 6th-century historian Jordanes, the Herules were driven from modern-day Denmark by the Danes, who were an offshoot of the Swedes. This migration is thought to have occurred around 250 AD.

Classical writers in antiquity mention several North Germanic tribes, in particular the Swedes, Danes, Geats, Gutes and Rugii. The North Germanic peoples are thought to have emerged as a distinct people in what is now southern Sweden in the early centuries AD.

The Danes would eventually settle all of Denmark, while many of its former inhabitants, including the Jutes and Angles, settled Britain and became known as the Anglo-Saxons. The Old English story Beowulf is a testimony to this connection.

The later Icelandic historian Snorri Sturluson begins his Heimskringla, a history of the Norse peoples, with the legends of ancient Sweden. This shows how important the Yngling dynasty of Gamla Uppsala was to the North Germanic peoples.

philosophy.text: Old Norse philosophy held that happiness could only be reached by living a life of virtue. Its key virtues were wisdom, self-control and personal independence, and they were seen as tightly interconnected. The best evidence for it is the Poetic Edda, especially the poem Hávamál.

Old Norse thinkers prized wisdom above wealth, and they thought wisdom could only be gained through experience. Travel was an important source of that experience. The author of the Hávamál points out that wealth is temporary while wisdom is eternal, and dismisses wealth as "the most fickle of friends".

Only a few sources for Germanic paganism were written by its own followers, so most were written by outsiders. Even so, scholars can reconstruct some basic beliefs. These include an origin myth, a myth of the end of the world, a belief that the inhabited world is a "middle-earth", and some ideas about fate and the afterlife.

Old Norse philosophy, despite coming from a warrior culture, held that even the lame, the armless, the deaf and the blind had a particular place in society. It taught that happiness comes only from a life of virtue, marked by wisdom, self-control and personal independence.

The Hávamál is a poem on social conduct attributed to Odin, the god of war and wisdom. It is considered the most important source on Old Norse philosophy. It has even been called the "Nicomachean Ethics of the North".

The earliest clear mention of Odin by name is on a C-bracteate found in Denmark in 2020. It may date to as early as the 400s and carries a Proto-Norse Elder Futhark inscription reading "He is Odin's man". Runic inscriptions in Danish bogs from the 4th or 5th century AD also use his later bynames.

Scholars such as Guðmundur Finnbogason and Sveinbjorn Johnson have noticed striking similarities between Old Norse philosophy and ancient Greek philosophy, especially that of Homer and Aristotle. These similarities appear to result from independent development rather than outside influence. Some researchers think Old Norse philosophy grew up largely in isolation.

It has been suggested that cult buildings were introduced into Scandinavia starting in the 3rd century. The idea is that they were modelled on the Christian churches then spreading across the Roman Empire. This was part of a range of political and religious changes that Nordic society was experiencing.

Graves containing bear claws, teeth and hides are found across the Germanic-speaking area, and in Scandinavia they are common from the 2nd to 5th centuries CE. They may be connected to warrior societies. Later Norse texts link the bear-associated berserkir and wolf-associated ulfheðnar to Odin.

Some archaeologists argue that Scandinavian "central places", settlements with religious, political, judicial and mercantile roles, were designed to mirror Old Norse cosmology. Their cultic place-names include Gudme (home of gods), Vä and Helgö (holy island). If so, ritual practice was tied directly to a wider worldview.

According to Lee M. Hollander, the Poetic Edda matters as much for understanding the ethical views of the Norse and other Germanic peoples as the Vedas do for Indian philosophy. He also compared it to the works of Homer, which help us understand ancient Greek philosophy.

culture.text: During the Nordic Bronze Age, grapes were grown in Scandinavia. The warm climate that began around 2700 BC was comparable to present-day central Germany and northern France. It allowed fairly dense population and good farming.

Scandinavia's rock carvings are among the most visible remains of its ancient culture. The period between 2300 and 500 BC was the most intensive time for carving, with images of agriculture, animals, nature, hunts, ships, ceremonies and warfare. Petroglyphs with themes of a sexual nature have also been found in Bohuslän, dating from 800 to 500 BC.

The Old Norse view of life was strongly fatalistic, since no man could ultimately escape his fate. This applied to everyone from kings to thralls, and it encouraged courage and fortitude. Stanza 77 of Hávamál says the only lasting thing is the noble name gained through noble deeds.

An early Scandinavian temple at Uppåkra, in modern Sweden, was a very large hall with two entrances. It was rebuilt seven times on exactly the same site between 200 and 950 CE. It was surrounded by animal bones and a few human bones.

Germanic peoples generally practiced cremation until the first century BCE, when limited inhumation burials began to appear. Grave goods, which could be broken or burnt on the pyre, included clothing, jewelry, food, drink, dishes and utensils. From the early 1st century CE, a minority of graves also held weapons.

After a long period of inhumation burials, people in the Nordic Bronze Age gradually switched to cremating their dead. With the Later Bronze Age (Period IV, 1100-900 BCE), the cremated remains were put in urns, though for a long time the urns were still placed in and around barrows. Researchers once thought urnfields appeared around 530 BCE, but new findings from the University of Kiel show it happened a century earlier.

Bog bodies from this era have been found in Denmark, Schleswig and southern Sweden. Alongside them were weapons, household wares and clothes of wool. At Nydam mosse in Schleswig, great ships made for rowing have been found from the 4th century.

The Iron Age brought a big change in Scandinavian life around the 6th and 5th centuries BC. Farming became more intensive around larger settlements, and slaves were introduced, which had been uncommon in the Bronze Age. Livestock, once grazed freely in wood pastures, were now placed in stables, probably to use manure more efficiently.

Scandinavian rock carvings survive in the thousands, most notably at Tanumshede in western Sweden and at Alta in Norway. They date from the period 2500 to 500 BC and remain visible to modern times. Some of those found in Bohuslän, dating from 800 to 500 BC, have themes of a sexual nature.

Petroglyphs with themes of a sexual nature have been found in Bohuslän, dating from 800 to 500 BC. They are part of the broader tradition of Scandinavian rock carvings, which also show ships, hunts and ceremonies.
